§05 — Expiry Is Not Fencing: Typed Leases and Kernel Write Exclusion

  • URLs: 1-Call Brief (/05/brief/) · Full (/05-expiry-is-not-fencing-typed-leases-and-kernel-write-exclusion/) · Raw Markdown (/05.md) · Parts (4): P1 P2 P3 P4
  • Thesis & Scope: Problem: An expired lease does not physically stop a stale worker or an uncooperative local writer from changing a resource. — Proves: Monotonic generations, current tenancy, typed scopes, and overlapping Win32 handle exclusion fence the write itself. — Scope: Use the Shared-Resource Lease & Kernel Fencing Challenge on one shared file or SQLite row.
  • The Two Hazards the Architecture Must Defeat: Subtopics: Hazard 1: The resurrected worker; Hazard 2: The uncooperative local writer — The refusal must happen at the resource. A wake-time check is not enough because authority can change after the wake. A heartbeat alone is not enough because a delayed heartbeat can arrive after succession.
  • 1. Six Typed Namespaces and Real Target Identity: Subtopics: Lexical paths are not kernel object identity — Leases are partitioned by resource class, not by an undifferentiated path string. Bare paths default to file:// for compatibility. A TypedScope contains the namespace and full resource_id; different namespaces never conflict with one… — Table Data: file://; Example resource: Exact files or directory hierarchies; Conflict rule: Canonical path-prefix conflicts; parent and child scopes overlap | session://; Example resource: Managed sessions and virtual resources such as sqlite.records/<target>; Conflict rule: Canonical session-resource prefix conflicts | window://; Example resource: GUI application…

§06 — Rollback Is Not Erasure: Dual-Tier Vaults and Ungated Quarantine

  • URLs: 1-Call Brief (/06/brief/) · Full (/06-rollback-is-not-erasure-dual-tier-vaults-and-ungated-quarantine/) · Raw Markdown (/06.md) · Parts (3): P1 P2 P3
  • Thesis & Scope: Problem: A single undo snapshot can destroy intermediate states and launder unauthorized writes into a clean baseline. — Proves: Primary certifies operational recovery while Amber preserves every intermediate and ungated state for forensics. — Scope: Use the Forensic Baseline & Quarantine Challenge on one file exposed to out-of-band edits.
  • 1. Why Single-Tier Undo Fails: Subtopics: Failure 1: The baseline is overwritten by the task itself; Failure 2: Ungated content becomes a trusted post-edit state — Single-slot backup systems fail in two distinct ways. The task has an undo button but no state 0 left. Worse, it cannot explain how state 3 was reached or which intermediate state was valid.
  • 2. The Dual-Tier Separation: Subtopics: Exhibit 6.1 — Dual-tier operational separation — Primary and Amber are not two copies of one backup. They answer different questions and have different failure and custody properties. Primary is the bounded operational store for rapid rollback.
  • One Checkout, Six Mutations, Two Truths: Consider one file checked out for remediation: The result is deliberately two truths: the file can return to a trusted baseline, while the evidence retains every intermediate and ungated state. — Items: Certified checkout. The lease and kernel handle are acquired. State 0 is written to Primary with its sidecar and capture-ledger binding, and archived to Amber with exact readback. If any step fails, both lease and handle are released.
  • 3. Primary: A Certified Operational Baseline: Subtopics: Scope sharding and identity; Monotonic version filenames; Readback before trust; Durable version binding; Exhibit 6.4 — A valid Primary capture binding — A file on disk in the Primary directory is not a baseline yet. It becomes one only after its bytes, sidecar, scope identity, and durable capture binding all verify. Each canonical file scope maps to .squad/vault/<fnv1a_16hex>/. — Items: every nonempty line must parse; | the destination must name the selected version exactly; | the record's canonical scope must resolve to the same file; | duplicate or conflicting bindings are refused; | digest, byte count, owner, and RFC 3339 timestamp must be well formed.
  • 4. Amber: Content-Addressed Forensic Objects: Subtopics: Atomic creation, deduplication, and exact readback — Amber stores raw bytes under: The first two digest characters create 256 shard directories. There is no Zstandard or .zst container. — Items: event: "amber_archived"; | capture kind, canonical scope and absolute source identity; | owner and intent; | SHA-256 and raw byte count; | timestamp and deduplication status.
  • 5. Fail-Closed Checkout Capture: Subtopics: Exhibit 6.2 — Fail-closed checkout capture state machine; Exhibit 6.5 — Checkout failure revokes tenancy — Checkout is a state machine, not a best-effort backup call. The lease and kernel handle are acquired first so the source cannot be casually changed during capture.
  • 6. Per-Mutation Amber Accumulation: Subtopics: Exhibit 6.6 — Amber edit snapshot — snapshot_edit_state captures the current bytes before a governed mutation and archives them only to Amber with kind: "edit_snapshot". Primary remains the state-0 undo baseline.
  • 7. The Active Bypass Sentinel: Subtopics: Exhibit 6.7 — bypass_detected — A guarded file can still be changed by a process outside the tool path. The active bypass sentinel scans active File leases and cross-indexes three observations: The bypass condition is: Path spellings are normalized so a junction, case… — Items: the lease's started_at timestamp; | the latest gated write found in snapshot.jsonl and file_edits.jsonl; | the file's current filesystem modification time.
  • 8. Release Verification and Ungated Quarantine: Subtopics: Exhibit 6.3 — Release verification and quarantine flow; Exhibit 6.8 — Release quarantine receipt — Release checks live on-disk bytes against the last authorized state. If a gated write occurred under the lease, the expected value is its post_sha256; otherwise the expected value is the checkout's pre-write FNV-1a hash and byte count.
  • 9. Restoration Is Another Governed Mutation: Subtopics: Governed restore; Console-exclusive operator rescue — A restore does not travel backward through history and delete the unauthorized act. It creates a new, evidence-bound transition from current state to a verified prior state.
  • 10. The Local-History and Non-Erasure Ceilings: Subtopics: Artifact integrity; Artifact survival; Downstream irreversibility — Recovery has three distinct assurance properties that must not be collapsed. SHA-256 and capture binding prove that stored bytes still match the evidence recorded for them. This detects substitution, corruption, and misleading provenance. — Items: an external API or webhook already dispatched; | a database query or third-party sync already committed; | confidential content already read or disclosed by another process; | another agent's reasoning, notifications, or subsequent state transitions already caused by the…
